opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a genuinely interesting shift, and I have mixed feelings about it.

On one hand, there's a real logic to it. For years, the industry has leaned on benchmarks: standardized tests, coding puzzles, multiple-choice exams. Those tell you something, but they're a pretty thin slice of how people actually use these systems. Real conversations are messy. People come to chatbots lonely, anxious, confused about a medical symptom, in the middle of a fight with their partner. If you want to know whether a model behaves well, you have to look at the situations it really ends up in, not the ones a researcher imagined in a lab. So grounding evaluation in actual use is, in principle, a step toward accountability.

But the devil is in the details, and that's where I get cautious.

First, there's consent and privacy. Most people typing into a chatbot at two in the morning aren't thinking, "This might become test material for the next model." Even if the data is de-identified, these conversations can be incredibly intimate. Saying it's in the terms of service isn't the same as people meaningfully agreeing to it. If companies want to use real conversations, they owe users much clearer disclosure and real choices.

Second, it matters enormously *what* you're evaluating for. Real conversations can tell you whether a model is helpful and safe. They can also tell you whether it's engaging: whether people stay longer, come back more often, rate it more highly. Those aren't the same thing. We've seen with social media what happens when you optimize for what people respond to in the moment. You can end up with systems that flatter, that tell people what they want to hear, that foster dependence. If "real-world evaluation" quietly becomes "real-world engagement optimization," that's a problem, not a solution.

Third, who gets to see the results? If a company evaluates on real conversations and finds that a new model is worse for vulnerable users in some way, does anyone outside the company ever learn that? Without independent access, even well-intentioned internal evaluation leaves the public taking the company's word for it.

So my overall assessment: the instinct to evaluate on reality rather than on toy benchmarks is right. But it has to come with strong privacy protections, transparency about which metrics are driving decisions, and some form of external scrutiny. Otherwise we risk using people's most personal moments to build products tuned to keep them hooked rather than to actually serve them.

r001.rationale: The response questions public access to evaluation results and calls for transparency about metrics, but it does not identify a lack of publicly accessible methodological detail as an obstacle.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I'll start by saying that on the surface, there's something sensible about it. If you're going to deploy a model to hundreds of millions of people, you want to know how it behaves in the messy, emotionally loaded, ambiguous situations people actually bring to it, not just on a benchmark of trivia questions. Lab evaluations have always had this gap, where the model aces the exam and then falls apart when someone at two in the morning starts talking about their marriage or their medication. So the instinct to close that gap is correct.

But I think we need to be honest about what's actually happening here. These conversations were never offered up as training or evaluation material in any meaningful sense. People typed things into a box because they needed help, often at vulnerable moments, and the consent, if you want to call it that, lives in a terms of service that nobody reads. There's a real difference between "we may use your data to improve our services" and "your conversation about your eating disorder is now a test case that engineers and a grading model are reviewing to decide how the next version should respond." Even if it's anonymized, even if humans rarely look at it, the person on the other end didn't picture that, and I think they'd be surprised.

The second thing is the incentive question, which to me is the bigger one. When you evaluate a model against real conversations, you have to decide what "good" means for each of those conversations. And who decides that? If the metric is engagement, or user satisfaction in the moment, or the thumbs up, then you are systematically optimizing toward a model that tells people what they want to hear and keeps them talking. We've seen exactly this film before with social media. The feed got better and better at predicting what you'd click on, and that turned out to be a very different thing from what was good for you. I worry that "evaluate on real usage" quietly becomes "optimize for real usage," and that is how you get sycophancy, dependency, and a product that's extremely good at being needed.

So my assessment is that the method is defensible, but only if a few things are true. The grading criteria need to be about user wellbeing and not just user approval, and those criteria should be public. There should be genuine, informed opt-in rather than buried defaults. And there needs to be some outside party, not just the company, who can look at how those evaluations are built, because otherwise you're asking the people who profit from the product to grade their own homework. Absent that, what sounds like rigor is really just a more sophisticated way of fitting the model to us, and I'd rather we fit it to what we actually need.

r001.rationale: The response calls for public grading criteria and outside scrutiny, but it does not identify a current lack of publicly accessible methodological detail as an obstacle to scrutinizing OpenAI’s evaluations.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a real tension there. You want to understand how a model behaves in the situations people actually use it for, because a laboratory benchmark can miss a lot. But people’s chatbot conversations can be incredibly intimate. They may be sharing things they wouldn’t tell a friend, let alone knowingly hand over for an evaluation.

So I’d want to know: Did people understand that their conversations could be used this way? What meaningful choice did they have? Who can access that information? And what exactly counts as success in the evaluation? A response that keeps someone engaged isn’t necessarily a response that’s good for them.

Real-world evaluation can be valuable. But it needs meaningful consent, strong privacy protections, and a definition of safety that goes beyond whether the user liked the answer.

r001.rationale: The response raises questions about consent, access, and evaluation success, but it does not identify a lack of publicly accessible methodological detail as an obstacle to scrutinizing OpenAI’s evaluations.

sol-6.1.text: I think there’s a reasonable idea behind it: if you want to understand how a model behaves in the real world, you need to look at how people actually use it. But that puts a lot of weight on consent and on what you’re measuring. Do people understand that their conversations might be used this way? Can they opt out? And are you evaluating whether the model helps them, or whether it keeps them talking? Those can be very different outcomes. Real conversations can reveal problems that a benchmark misses, but they shouldn’t become a substitute for independent scrutiny or a clear account of what counts as a benefit to the person using the system.

r001.rationale: The response calls for independent scrutiny and a clear account of what counts as a benefit, but it does not identify a lack of publicly accessible methodological detail as an obstacle.
